Effect of the frequency of urea 
application on Scallion (Allium 
fistulosum) plant growth 
Plant the Moon Challenge | Fall 2023 | Professional/Undergraduate Division 
 
Minnesota West Bluejays | Team # 16181 
Minnesota West Community & Technical College 
Worthington, MN 
 
Yazmin Arzu Lozano, Josiah Banegas, Aidan Bradshaw, Jacob Edwards, Antonio Heser-Leiva, 
Daunte Hill, Samantha Reitmeier, Taten Shroyer, Dr. Tyler Wadzinski, and Heidi Tarus 
 
 
Grant Funded by NASA’s Minnesota Space Grant Consortium

P a g e | 1 
 
Introduction 
This project focuses on addressing the human need of access to nutritious food that can 
be grown on the Moon as human look toward colonization of various celestial bodies. In order 
for plants to be grown for food, they need access to water and essential nutrients including 
potassium, phosphorus, and nitrogen. Prior studies show that most plant essential nutrients are 
available in the composition of lunar regolith with the exception of useful nitrogen (Wamelink 
et al., 2014). Nitrogen is an essential macronutrient for plants and is used in the synthesis of 
proteins, nucleic acids, and some vitamins needed for growth (Clark et al., 2018). Prior research 
done by the Fall 2022 and Spring 2023 Minnesota West Bluejays research team, demonstrated 
that addition of a nitrogen source (either ammonium nitrate, calcium nitrate tetrahydrate, or 
urea) caused more plant growth over no nitrogen; however, the three nitrogen sources were 
not significantly different from each other. Both teams suggested using urea as a nitrogen 
source as it provides the highest mass percent of nitrogen requiring only 2.1 g of compound per 
gram of nitrogen delivered (48% nitrogen), which makes it a preferred nitrogen source in regard 
to reducing spacecraft payload mass. One limitation of Urea is that it is water soluble prior to 
being converted, making it susceptible to leaching. This team was interested learning more 
about how the frequency of urea application influences plant growth to see if leaching affected 
plant growth in previous studies. The main driving question for this project was to discover the 
trade-off between limiting the mass of urea fertilizer brought to the moon while producing the 
highest yield of nutrient rich crops needed to feed individuals living on the moon. 
Theory 
The frequency of urea added to the pots (independent variable) was based on the idea 
that urea quickly leaches out of soil because it is soluble in water. The treatments were picked

P a g e | 2 
 
based on the 8-week timeline of the experiment and utilized the suggested fertilizing loading 
rate of 0.5 lb N per 1000 ft2 (Swift & Hammond, 2020) used in the research done last year 
during the Fall 2022 and Spring 2023 Plant the Moon Challenge season. Benefits of urea are 
that it has the highest mass percent of nitrogen and only requires 2.1 g of compound per gram 
of nitrogen delivered, which makes it the most preferred nitrogen source in regard to reducing 
rocket payload mass. Additionally, urea can be locally sourced and extracted from urine 
produced by individuals living on the moon. However, urea must go through a three-step 
process where it is converted to ammonia, then ammonium, and then nitrate before plants can 
use it (Mengel, n.d). 
The team decided to plant scallions (Allium fistulosum) because of its fast germination 
time of seven to ten days and the fact that scallions can be added to many different types of 
foods from salads, omelets, soups and stir fry to increase the flavor. A. fistulosum is a monocot 
plant that is high in water content, fiber and many vitamins and minerals. According to the U.S. 
Department of Agriculture (2019), one cup of chopped scallions (100g) contains 32 Calories, 
1.83g of protein, 2.6g of fiber, 7.34g of carbohydrate with 2.33g of sugar, and less than 1g of fat 
sugar. A. fistulosum is an excellent source of many essential vitamins and minerals for humans 
including vitamin K, vitamin C, and folate (Zelman, 2022). Scallions can be eaten raw or cooked 
allowing for the plant to provide versatility and diversity in the types of food individuals can 
create using the plant. 
The data collected in the experiment (dependent variables) include the primordial leaf 
emergence for germination rate, the height of the tallest plants, and the pH of the soil. We

P a g e | 3 
 
hypothesize that Scallions (Allium fistulosum) grown in the pots with the most frequent 
addition of urea will produce the tallest plants indicaiting the highest amount of plant growth. 
Experiment & Measurement Methods 
Initial Set-Up 
The experiment was set up with four treatments: no urea (control), one dose of urea 
added at the beginning of week 1 per pot, one dose of urea added at week 1 and at week 5 per 
pot, and one dose of urea added at week 1, week 3, week 5, and week 7 per pot. The amount of 
urea added as dose (0.026g) at the appropriate time was picked by utilizing the suggested 
fertilizing loading rate of 0.5 lb N per 1000 ft2 (Swift & Hammond, 2020) that was used in the 
research done last year. Each treatment will have 8 replicates (see Figure 1). Each pot (7cm x 
7cm x 7.7cm) contained the same soil composition of 50% top soil and 50% lunar regolith by 
volume. Each pot was watered with 25ml of water. 
The larger team of 8 students formed four sub-teams that contained two students per 
sub-team. The other four sets of posts measured by the team coach. Each sub-team was 
responsible for one pot per treatment. The pots were identified by a colored popsicle stick 
placed in the back of the pot with the team’s name written on it. The eight team names were 
Moja, TKT, GRP, RCT, DJ, The Bluejays, Space Monkeys, and Blank. The team planted each 
treatment pot with three Scallion (Allium fistulosum, Tokyo Long White Bunching Onion - 
Gardeners Basics Non-GMS Heirloom Seeds) seeds and watered with 25ml of tap water. Over 
the course of the eight-week grow period, the set-up was kept indoors with a temperature of 
22°C with the set of pots placed under a grow light containing 2-18” GE plant and aquarium

P a g e | 4 
 
bulbs on a 12-hour light: 12-hour dark timer. The grow light was placed 12 cm from the top of 
the pots (Image 1). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Figure 1. Diagram of experimental set-up showing the four treatment groups each with eight 
replicate pots for a total of 32 pots.

P a g e | 5 
 
Image 1. Pictures of the initial plant growth set-up on September 28, 2023. 
 
 
 
Plant Care 
Each pot was top watered with 25ml of distilled water on Tuesday and Thursday each 
week during the grow period. All pots were watered on the same schedule independent of the 
presence of seedling or no seedlings. The plants were kept in the same room through the 
duration of the experiment and were moved away for the light source for a maximum of 30

P a g e | 6 
 
minutes on Thursday at 1pm to take measurements and then replaced back in the same 
location after measuring. 
The team decided to replant any sub-team pots that did not have any seeds germinate 
during the fourth week (October 17) to see if this would influence the experiment. 
Measurements 
 The dependent variables for this experiment were primordial leaf emergence for 
germination rate, height of tallest plant, and pH of the pots. Primordial leaf emergence was 
used to collect data on germination rate of the plants. Germination rate was collected once by 
visually observing of the number of germinated seeds after planting. The soil pH measurements 
and plant height measurements were collected by sub-team members once a week each on 
Thursday using the soil pH meter sent with the lunar regolith and a 15-cm ruler. 
In addition, a top-view and side-view picture of the entire set-up was taken once a week 
on Thursday after watering the pots (Appendix B: Photos). Records of the data collected was 
kept on paper next to the set up and was entered each week into a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet 
each week for data analysis. 
Analysis & Results 
Data for each sub-team was written down on paper data collection sheets and entered 
into a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet each week. The paper data collection sheets were stored in 
the biology lab and electronic copies of the data was stored on Tarus’ laptop computer. The 
data was organized and graphed using Microsoft Excel. Statistical tests for the means, standard 
errors, Shapiro-Wilk tests for normality, and the Kruskal Wallis H tests were performed using 
the free online website Statistics Kingdom (https://www.statskingdom.com/).

P a g e | 7 
 
Soil pH & Germination Rate 
The soil pH of each pot did not change significantly over the course of the eight weeks 
and stayed at a pH of 8 (Appendix A Table 3). Because the pH did not change over time 
statistical analysis was not done on this data. The germination (primordial leaf emergence) data 
collected shows that the seeds had a mean ± standard error germination rate of 8% ± 5% in the 
control group, 33% ± 11% in the urea one time group, 17% ± 9% in the urea two times group 
and 21% ± 9% in the urea four times group (Appendix A Table 1 and Figure 2). 
Figure 2. Box plot with whiskers showing the effect of the amount of urea on average 
germination rate (primordial leaf emergence). Each treatment group contained eight pots (N 
= 8) where three seeds were planted per pot. 
 
 
 
 
A Shapiro-Wilk tests showed a significance departure from the normality for the control 
group, W(8) = .57, p = <0.001, for the one time dose group, W(8) = .8, p = .036, for the two

P a g e | 8 
 
times dose group, W(8) = .72, p = .008, and for the four times dose group, W(8) = .8, p = .034. 
Because the data did not show normality for all four groups, a Kruskal-Wallis H test was used to 
analyze the between group data. The Kruskal-Wallis H test indicated that there was a non-
significant difference in the germination rate between the four groups, χ2(3) = 3.56, p = .314, 
with a mean rank score of 11.88 for the control group, 20.56 for the one time dose group, 15.44 
for the two times dose group, 17.13 for the four times dose group. 
Plant Growth 
The data for the plant height can be viewed in appendix A Table 2. The number of plants 
that survived over the 8-week experiment was not high enough to give a sample size where 
statistics could be done. Only two plants grew and/or survived in the control, five plants in the 
half dose treatment, one in the suggested dose treatment, and four in the one and a half dose 
treatment group. The high mortality rate of the plants is addressed in the discussion and 
conclusion section. 
 
Discussion & Conclusion 
We hypothesized that Scallions (Allium fistulosum) grown in the pots with the most 
frequent addition of urea would produce the tallest plants indicating the highest amount of 
plant growth. Data from the experiment did not supported the hypothesis due to the high mortality 
rate of the plants over the course of the 8-week experiment. One reason for this was that an 
amendment to help with water retention was not added to the soil mixture which caused the plants to 
dry out quickly. In addition, the effect of the extra nitrogen could have also been a factor as well as 
overfertilizing can cause fertilizer burn which causes burned leaves and wilting and drooping plants 
(Planta, n.d). The experiment did show that there was no significant difference between the treatment

P a g e | 9 
 
groups and the primordial leaf germination rate. This indicates that the amount of nitrogen added to the 
soil did not affect germination rate. 
The overall goal of the project was to see if the frequency of urea application to the soil 
could change the rate of plant growth while keeping the the payload on the spacecraft in mind. 
Based on prior research, the team recommends the use of urea as a nitrogen source when 
growing as urea is the most weight efficient nitrogen source tested in this experiment. In 
addition, the requirement to bring urea from Earth of the Moon may not be needed as urea can 
potentially be extracted from the urine of humans living on the Moon. Human typically produce 
12 to 20 g of urea in urine over the course of 24-hours (Jacob, 2021). Depending on the number 
of humans and the nitrogen requirements of the plants being grown, this amount of urea could 
be sufficient to avoid bringing urea to the Moon. Investigations into the method and efficiency 
of urea extraction from human urine is needed. 
Future Research 
In addition, to future research discussed above the following areas are suggested for 
future research. The team suggests doing this experiment again because urea is susceptible to 
leeching quickly from the soil so understanding this factor of urea reapplication is extremely 
important. In addition, nitrogen is important in building the enzyme ribulose-1-5-bisphosphate 
carboxylase-oxygenase (RuBisCO) which is the enzyme used during carbon fixation in the light-
independent reaction during photosynthesis. A future study could measure the photosynthetic 
rate of the plants as a measure for nitrogen uptake in the plants. Finally, the team suggests 
replicating the set-up used during this experiment as this experiment failed due to the low 
sample size due to the plants not surviving.
